terms.definition: Bringing market forces of supply, demand, competition and choice into education.
terms.examiner: The 1988 Education Reform Act is the key starting point. Explain its effect on inequality, not just what it is.

terms.definition: Rule by parents: the idea that parents, as consumers, drive education through school choice.
terms.examiner: David's term. Evaluate with Ball: the 'choice' mainly benefits middle-class parents.

terms.definition: Published rankings of schools by results, such as GCSE scores.
terms.examiner: Link them to cream-skimming and silt-shifting: schools want pupils who will raise their ranking.

terms.definition: Popular schools selecting the most able pupils, who are mostly middle class.
terms.examiner: Bartlett's term, usually paired with silt-shifting.

terms.definition: Schools avoiding pupils with learning difficulties or behaviour problems who might lower results.
terms.examiner: Bartlett. Use it to explain how marketisation reproduces inequality.

terms.definition: Paying schools a fixed sum for each pupil, so popular schools get more money.
terms.examiner: Shows how inequality between schools grows: oversubscribed schools gain, unpopular ones lose.

terms.definition: Admitting pupils on the basis of ability, for example by the eleven-plus exam in the tripartite system.
terms.examiner: Know the 1944 tripartite system and the 1965 move to comprehensives. Evaluate both from functionalist and Marxist views.

terms.definition: Non-selective state schools that take pupils of all abilities.
terms.examiner: Functionalists see it as promoting meritocracy; Marxists point out that streaming kept inequality inside the school.

terms.definition: State-funded schools run independently of the local authority, with control over the curriculum and pay.
terms.examiner: A post-2010 expansion. Link to fragmentation and to the privatisation of education.

terms.definition: The transfer of public services and assets to private companies, for example academy chains and outsourced exam services.
terms.examiner: Ball and Whitty. Connect it to globalisation: some providers are multinational companies.

terms.definition: Policies that put extra resources into schools or areas with disadvantaged pupils.
terms.examiner: Examples: Education Action Zones, Sure Start, the pupil premium. Evaluate their effect on the class gap.

terms.definition: Ball's description of policy that breaks up local authority control while giving central government more power.
terms.examiner: Useful in essays on post-2010 policy, alongside academies and free schools.
